# macOS developer security setup

A practical baseline for a developer Mac in 2026. It assumes you install packages from npm and PyPI
daily, clone repos you did not write, and let AI coding agents run commands. Those three things are
how developer machines get owned today, and most of the defences below are free.

Legend: **MUST** do this week · **SHOULD** do this month · **NICE** when you get to it · **$** costs money.

---

## 0. Threat model, in one paragraph

Nobody is going to brute-force your laptop. You will be compromised by (a) a package whose latest
version was hijacked an hour ago, (b) a repository that runs code the moment you open it or
`npm install` it (North Korea-linked fake job-interview campaigns, Contagious Interview and PolinRider among
them, send developers such repos, and their stealers take browser logins, wallets and keys), (c) a web page that tells you to
paste a command into Terminal (ClickFix / AMOS stealer), or (d) an AI agent that, prompted by text in
a repo, installs or runs something it should not. Everything below is layered against those four.

---

## 1. The OS itself (all free, all MUST)

| Setting | Where | Why |
|---|---|---|
| FileVault on | System Settings → Privacy & Security | Lost laptop = lost disk, not lost data |
| Firewall on + stealth mode | Privacy & Security → Firewall | Nothing on the LAN can probe you |
| Gatekeeper left on, never `spctl --master-disable` | default | Blocks unsigned downloads |
| Automatic updates on, including security responses | General → Software Update | Most macOS exploits in the wild are already patched |
| AirPlay Receiver, Remote Login, Remote Management, File Sharing: off | General → AirDrop & Handoff / Sharing | Listening services you don't use |
| Screen lock immediately, Touch ID for sudo | Lock Screen / `/etc/pam.d/sudo_local` | |
| Browser password manager off, a password manager on (1Password, Bitwarden or Apple Passwords) | each browser | Stealers read browser stores from disk; they cannot read a locked vault |
| Remote-access tools you don't actively use (TeamViewer, AnyDesk, RustDesk) uninstalled with the vendor uninstaller | Terminal | They leave authorization plugins and privileged helpers behind — root-level persistence you'll see in every KnockKnock run |

Check them in one go: `csrutil status`, `fdesetup isactive`, `spctl --status`,
`/usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --getglobalstate --getstealthmode`.

---

## 2. Install-time protection for npm / PyPI (the layer that matters most)

**MUST: [Aikido Safe Chain](https://github.com/AikidoSec/safe-chain)** (free, open source).
Wraps `npm npx pnpm yarn bun pip pip3 python -m pip uv uvx poetry pipx pdm`. Two things it does:
blocks packages on Aikido's malware feed, and refuses any version published less than 48 hours ago.
The second one is the whole trick: hijacked versions are almost always yanked within hours.

Install it properly, which the installer alone does not do:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://github.com/AikidoSec/safe-chain/releases/download/<version>/install-safe-chain.sh -o /tmp/i.sh
# verify the sha256 against the README before running it
sh /tmp/i.sh          # interactive-shell aliases
sh /tmp/i.sh --ci     # PATH shims in ~/.safe-chain/shims, for scripts, IDEs and agents
```

Then make the shims win **everywhere**, not just in your terminal:

- Put `~/.safe-chain/shims` first on PATH at the **end** of `~/.zshrc` **and** `~/.zprofile`
  (login shells like `zsh -lc`, which Codex uses, never read `.zshrc`; `/etc/zprofile` reorders PATH
  after `.zshenv`). Same for `~/.bashrc` / `~/.bash_profile` if you use bash.
- `launchctl setenv PATH "$HOME/.safe-chain/shims:…"` from a login LaunchAgent, so GUI apps,
  editors and agents launched from the Dock inherit it.
- Pin the age gate in the environment: `export SAFE_CHAIN_MINIMUM_PACKAGE_AGE_HOURS=48` in
  `~/.zshenv`. A repo can ship a `.aikido` file that lowers the gate; the environment variable wins.
- Prove it: `npm install --no-save safe-chain-test` must be refused, `npm safe-chain-verify` must
  say OK, and `/usr/bin/which npm` must print the shim from `zsh -lc`, `zsh -c`, `bash -lc`, `bash -c`
  and from `env -i HOME=$HOME /bin/zsh -lc '…'`.

To install something genuinely fresh, lower the gate for that one command in your own terminal:
`SAFE_CHAIN_MINIMUM_PACKAGE_AGE_HOURS=0 npm i <pkg>`. Never set it permanently, never from an agent.

**SHOULD:** `pnpm` and `bun` block install scripts by default; keep that. Don't set
`ignore-scripts=true` globally for npm unless you know your native deps (esbuild, sharp, prisma,
electron) and are ready to `npm rebuild` them. **SHOULD:** use `corepack` for pnpm/yarn so each
repo's pinned version is used. **NICE:** Safe Chain does not cover `cargo`, `go install`, `gem`,
`brew`, `deno` — use `cargo install --locked`, pin Homebrew formulae, and treat those as unscanned.

---

## 3. Repositories you clone (MUST read, SHOULD automate)

A poisoned repo does not need `npm install` to hurt you:

- `.vscode/tasks.json` with `"runOn": "folderOpen"` runs when you open the folder. **MUST:** set
  `"task.allowAutomaticTasks": "off"` in VS Code and Cursor.
- A payload appended after a long run of blank space at the end of a config file (`postcss.config.mjs`,
  `tailwind.config.js` and similar) is out of sight when you open the file, and runs when the tool loads it.
- `.husky/`, `lefthook.yml`, `.git/hooks` run on your next commit.
- `.claude/settings.json`, `.codex/hooks.json`, `.cursor/hooks.json` can add hooks that run on every
  agent session. The ChainDrop npm worm (August 2026) wrote a session-start hook into `.claude/settings.json`
  ([Pillar Security](https://www.pillar.security/blog/chaindrop-when-opening-a-repository-becomes-execution),
  [Zscaler](https://zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/tracking-shai-hulud-inside-chaindrop-npm-worm)).
- `.npmrc` / `uv.toml` / `pyproject.toml` can point the package manager at an attacker's registry.
- A "font" file that is actually JavaScript, run as `node public/fonts/fa-solid.woff2`.

**SHOULD:** a global git hook (`git config --global hook.<name>.event post-checkout` +
`post-merge` + `post-rewrite`, git ≥ 2.54) that scans the files a clone/pull/checkout just brought
in for exactly those patterns and shows a notification before you run anything. The public IOC pack
for PolinRider lives at [OpenSourceMalware/PolinRider](https://github.com/OpenSourceMalware/PolinRider).
**MUST:** never run an interview take-home, a "demo project" from a recruiter, or a random GitHub
project on your main user account. Use a VM or container (§8).

**SHOULD:** `git config --global push.default simple`, no `--force` aliases, branch protection
with "no force push" on every repo you own. PolinRider spreads by rewriting a repo's newest commit, keeping its
author, date and message, and force-pushing it to every repo the infected developer can push to; disallowing
force-push defeats the technique, not just the signature.

## 4. AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Zed…)

Agents are not malicious, but they are suggestible and they run with your credentials. A line of
text in a README is enough to make one run `curl … | sh`. Treat the agent as an untrusted operator:

- **MUST:** the shims-first PATH from §2 must apply to the agent's shell. Check from inside each
  agent: `/usr/bin/which npm` → shim; `npm install --no-save safe-chain-test` → refused.
- **MUST:** a pre-command hook that refuses the obvious bypasses: a package manager by full path
  (`/opt/homebrew/bin/npm`, `.venv/bin/pip`), `PATH=` or `env -i` rewrites, `SAFE_CHAIN_*=0`,
  `--safe-chain-*` flags, `safe-chain uninstall`, registry overrides, `curl | sh`, `node file.woff2`,
  and any write to the files that enforce all of this (rc files, the hook config, the hook itself).
  Claude Code: `hooks.PreToolUse` on `Bash` and `Write|Edit|MultiEdit` with `… || exit 2` so a broken
  hook fails closed. Codex: `~/.codex/hooks.json` plus `~/.codex/rules/*.rules` with
  `prefix_rule(decision="forbidden")` for each real package-manager path. OpenCode: a plugin on
  `tool.execute.before`. Zed: `agent.tool_permissions.tools.terminal.always_deny`.
  The hook is pattern matching, not a sandbox; it stops an agent that slips or is talked into it.
- **MUST:** deny the agent edits to its own controls (`permissions.deny` → `Edit(~/.claude/settings.json)`,
  `Edit(~/.zprofile)`, …) and never accept a security baseline from an agent.
- **MUST:** put the same controls in a root-owned tier the agent cannot reach, because everything
  above lives in files your own user can write. Copy the hook script to
  `/usr/local/lib/safe-chain-agent/` (root:wheel 755), then
  `/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json` (root:wheel 644) with the hooks
  pointing at that copy, the deny list and `"permissions": {"disableBypassPermissionsMode": "disable"}`;
  managed settings win over user and project settings. For Codex, `/etc/codex/requirements.toml`
  with `allowed_sandbox_modes = ["read-only", "workspace-write"]` and the off-switches as
  `[rules] prefix_rules` (`safe-chain uninstall`, `env -i`, …). Deny rules apply even under
  `--dangerously-skip-permissions`. After every hook update, re-copy the root version: the weekly
  check should diff the two. This protects against the agent, not against someone with your
  admin password.
- Keep the agent autonomous. The point is a filter on *what* it installs and *which files* it may
  touch, not a sandbox-only or approve-every-command mode; those get switched off within a week.
  Don't set `allowManagedHooksOnly` unless every hook you rely on is in the managed file too.
  The Codex requirements above are not that mode: `workspace-write` lets Codex work on its own inside the
  project, and only `danger-full-access`, which switches its sandbox off entirely, is ruled out. That root-owned
  file is the one control a Codex session can't rewrite for itself.
- **SHOULD:** pin MCP servers (`npx -y pkg@1.2.3`, not `@latest`); they start on every session.
- **SHOULD:** review project-level agent settings and hooks before opening a cloned repo in an agent.
- **NICE:** Claude Code `sandbox` (macOS Seatbelt) and Codex permission profiles for kernel-enforced
  filesystem and network limits — only if you accept the breakage (`docker`, `gh`, `terraform`,
  `osascript` need exclusions) and the slower loop.

## 6. Secrets: assume the payload runs, make it find nothing

- **MUST:** keep SSH keys in a protected SSH agent: [1Password](https://1password.com/)'s ($), free
  [Secretive](https://github.com/maxgoedjen/secretive) (keys made in the Secure Enclave) or the free
  [Bitwarden](https://bitwarden.com/help/ssh-agent/) agent. Import or create your keys there, delete the files from
  `~/.ssh`, and every use needs your approval. A stealer reading `~/.ssh` gets nothing. Another agent counts too,
  recorded as an accepted decision. Minimum fallback: `ssh-keygen -p -f ~/.ssh/<key>` on every key.
- **MUST:** no plaintext keys lying around. Audit with
  `fd -H -t f '(\.pem|\.key|credentials|sa-key.*\.json|\.env)$' ~ -E Library -E node_modules`.
  Anything in `~/Downloads` or `~` itself is a leak waiting to happen.
- **MUST:** GitHub tokens are the blast radius. `gh auth login` gives a classic OAuth token with full
  `repo` scope (and often `workflow` / `admin:org`); any process running as you can read it with
  `gh auth token`. Use fine-grained PATs, scoped to the org, with an expiry; let your org restrict
  classic tokens. Same for cloud CLIs: short-lived SSO sessions, not long-lived keys.
- **SHOULD:** [gitleaks](https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks) as a pre-commit hook and
  `gitleaks git <repo>` on anything you inherit; [git-filter-repo](https://github.com/newren/git-filter-repo)
  to purge what you find; GitHub secret-scanning push protection on your orgs ($, Team plan add-on).
- **SHOULD:** rotate on a schedule, not on an incident. Keys and tokens older than a year are
  probably in a backup, a transcript or a log somewhere.
- **NICE:** AI-agent transcripts (`~/.claude/projects`, `~/.codex/sessions`, OpenCode's DB) contain
  every secret you ever pasted. Scrub them weekly or exclude them from backups.
- **$ NICE:** two [YubiKeys](https://www.yubico.com/) (~$50 each) as GitHub / Google / 1Password
  second factors; passkeys where offered.

## 10. Automate it, or it decays (SHOULD)

Two launchd jobs with a Notification Center banner on failure, and a daily health check that alerts
when a job is unloaded, failing or overdue:

- **Weekly update (Mon):** `brew update && brew upgrade && brew vulns`, Safe Chain self-update
  (pinned, checksum-verified), `uv tool upgrade --all`, global npm, nuclei templates, transcript scrub,
  90-day log retention.
- **Weekly security check (Wed):** posture (§1) · Safe Chain still first on PATH in every shell type,
  test package still refused · agent hooks still registered, control files unchanged (sha256 vs
  baseline) · persistence diff (LaunchAgents/Daemons, login items, cron, agent hooks, KnockKnock) ·
  non-loopback listeners diff · IOC sweep of the machine and repos · git-scan findings · SSH keys
  without passphrase. New entries alert until **you** accept them into the baseline.

Keep the scripts under `~/.local/bin`, logs under `~/.local/var/log`, and make the security check
refuse to accept a baseline from an agent.

# If fortkeep finds signs of malware

Read this whole page first. Step 1 takes your Mac off the internet, and after that your coding agent can't help.
It is written for anyone, and works without fortkeep or an agent. Stay calm: going step by step matters more than
going fast.

## 1. Take the Mac off the network

Turn off Wi-Fi (the Wi-Fi icon in the menu bar, or Control Center) and unplug any network cable. That cuts off
anything that is sending your data out or taking orders from outside.

Leave the Mac switched on, and don't restart it unless the people helping you say so: what is running now can show
what happened.

## 2. Stop using this Mac

Don't type passwords on it, don't sign in to anything, and don't open the suspicious project, file or app again.

## 3. Change your passwords and keys from a clean device

Use your phone or another computer you trust, never this Mac: anything you type here may be read. Do the ones you
actually use, in this order:

1. GitHub and cloud accounts (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, and so on): revoke your access tokens and keys, then change
   the passwords.
2. SSH keys: remove this Mac's public keys from GitHub and from the servers they open. You'll make new keys later,
   on a clean machine.
3. Sign out everywhere: most services (Google, GitHub, Slack, your email) have a "sign out of all sessions" option.
4. Crypto wallets, if a wallet was ever on this Mac: move the funds to a new wallet created on a clean device.
5. Passwords and keys kept in project files (such as `.env` files): replace each one with the service that issued it.

## 4. Get help

- **A work Mac:** tell your employer's IT or security team now. Say what you ran or opened, and when. They decide
  what happens next; follow them rather than this page.
- **Your own Mac:** contact an incident-response service (a company that investigates break-ins on computers). If
  you can't, at least wait to decide on step 5 until you've rotated everything in step 3.

## 5. Don't wipe it yet

Erasing or reinstalling the Mac destroys the evidence of what was taken and how. Decide that with the people helping
you. Keep the suspicious file or project: don't delete it, don't open it.

## 6. Report it

- The bad package to its registry's security team (npm or PyPI), and the repo or package to
  [OpenSourceMalware](https://opensourcemalware.com), so others are warned.
- A flaw in fortkeep itself (a check that missed something, or a false alarm you can reproduce): see
  [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md).

## Was it a false alarm?

One warning has an everyday cause: "agent control files changed since your baseline" also appears when you, or an
app update, changed one of those files (such as `~/.zshrc`). If you recognise every change it lists, it is not an
emergency: open the Terminal app, go to the fortkeep folder and type `checks/baseline.sh accept`. If you don't
recognise a change, treat it as real and start at step 1.

# When a security tool stops a check

Antivirus and endpoint protection (EDR: CrowdStrike Falcon, Microsoft Defender, SentinelOne, Bitdefender and others)
watch what programs read, not just what they run. A few fortkeep checks read the same places an infostealer reads, so
a security tool may kill them. The check then shows:

> ! ERROR · Something outside fortkeep stopped this check (signal KILL), most likely a security tool running on this
> Mac: Falcon Sensor. …

The Mac is no less safe because of it, and the rest of the review still counts. That one check has no answer until
the security tool lets it run.

## Which checks, and why they look suspicious

Every check only reads, and each lesson's "What the agent is doing" line (`teach/<ID>.md`) says what. These read
places that infostealers also read:

| Check | What it reads | What a security tool may see |
|---|---|---|
| BL-BR-04 | Each browser profile's extension folders, for crypto-wallet extension IDs | A script walking browser profiles for wallets: credential or wallet theft ("Data from Local System") |
| BL-BR-01, BL-BR-02, BL-BR-03 | Each browser profile's settings, its extension list and the count of saved passwords | Reading browser profile and login data |
| BL-SE-02 | The key files in `~/.ssh`, opened with an empty passphrase to see if each has one | Access to private keys |
| BL-SE-03 | Key and secret files (`.pem`, `.key`, `.p12`, `.env`, `credentials`, `id_*`…) up to four folders deep in Desktop, Documents and Downloads, and at the top of your home folder; it opens each `.pem` and `.key` file to see if it holds a private key | A sweep for keys and secrets |
| GD-RT-03 | Running programs' command lines, your network connections, start-up files, scheduled jobs and temporary folders | Process and network discovery |

So far only BL-BR-04 has been seen killed, by CrowdStrike Falcon. Any of these could be on another Mac.

The repo scanner is a separate program: `/scan`, `fortkeep scan` and the weekly repo sweep (GD-RC-01) run it as
`/usr/bin/python3 -I /Users/<you>/.local/share/fortkeep/fixes/files/git-scan-new-files`. It reads each git repo's
files, hooks and history, looking for known malware markers. If a security tool kills it, `/scan` says the scan is
incomplete and GD-RC-01 says "The repo scanner failed (exit 137)". Ask for the same narrow exclusion as below, with
that command line.

## What to ask for: this one check, nothing wider

Ask whoever manages the security tool to **exclude the one check that was stopped, for the one detection that fired,
on your Mac only**. The narrowest form is the check's command line, exactly as fortkeep starts it:

```
/bin/bash -p /Users/<you>/.local/share/fortkeep/checks/macos/<ID>.sh
```

Keep the `-p`. Without it, bash runs a file named by the `BASH_ENV` variable before the check, so anything that can
start that command line could run its own code inside the excluded process. Sometimes the security tool stops a
program the check started (`sqlite3`, `ssh-keygen`, `jq`) rather than the check itself. The detection names the
process it stopped: the exclusion uses that process's file and command line.

Turn these down, even if they are quicker:

- **The whole fortkeep folder**, or your home folder. You can write to `~/.local/share/fortkeep`, and so can
  anything running as you. Excluding the folder would let anything put in it past the security tool.
- **A process-name exclusion for `bash`**, which would cover every shell script on the Mac.
- **Turning off a protection** (behavioural, machine learning) or moving the Mac to a lighter policy.
- **Turning the security tool off** to get the check to run.

If the tool can't exclude anything narrower than a folder, leave the check as `! ERROR`. One check with no answer
is better than a hole in the security tool.

An exclusion for one script still trusts that script to stay as released, and anything running as you can change it.
fortkeep compares its folder with the signed release when an agent session starts and before an update, and warns
about any file that changed. It notices a replaced check only if the change is still there at one of those moments.

## A message to forward

On a work Mac, send this to your IT or security team, with the check's ID and the time of its run filled in:

> fortkeep (https://github.com/b0dea/fortkeep), an open-source security checkup I run on my Mac, had one check stopped
> by our endpoint protection. It's a false positive: the check is a read-only shell script that looks for

> - Check: `<ID>`, at `/Users/<you>/.local/share/fortkeep/checks/macos/<ID>.sh`
> - Command line: `/bin/bash -p /Users/<you>/.local/share/fortkeep/checks/macos/<ID>.sh`
> - When: `<date and time of the run>`
>
> Could you add an exclusion for that command line only, for the detection that fired, on my Mac only? Please don't
> exclude the whole fortkeep folder: I can write to it, so that would open a gap. The script's source is in the repo

## On your own Mac

Open the security tool's threat history or quarantine and find the detection for fortkeep's check. If it lets you
allow that one detection or that one file, do that. If it only offers to allow a folder, leave the check as an

## Per tool

**CrowdStrike Falcon.** BL-BR-04 shows up as a detection with tactic "Collection", technique "Data from Local
System" and "Prevention, process killed". An admin adds an **IOA exclusion** for that detection's pattern, scoped to
your Mac's host group, with:

- Image filename: `/bin/bash`
- Command line: `/bin/bash -p /Users/<you>/\.local/share/fortkeep/checks/macos/BL-BR-04\.sh`

An IOA exclusion skips only that pattern for that command line. A sensor visibility or machine-learning exclusion is
far wider and isn't needed.

**Other tools.** Give your admin the detection's name and time, and ask for that tool's narrowest exclusion: one that
matches the command line above, for that detection only, on your Mac only. If you find exact steps for a tool,
please add them here in a pull request.

# Threat model

fortkeep guards one thing: a coding agent, in a session a person started to check their Mac, doing something the
person didn't approve. It stops agent mistakes, and prompt injection that asks the agent for a guarded action: text in
a repo, a web page or scan output telling it to run, read or change something.

It does not stop:

- a malicious or modified agent program. The guards are hooks the agent program runs; a program that skips them
  skips them.
- anything already running as the person's macOS user. That can change any file the user can, fortkeep's included:
  its guards, approvals, results and the start-up files its fixes edit.

fortkeep is not an antivirus and not a sandbox. Its checks report how the Mac is set up; they don't block anything.

## A person's session

A person's session is any session that isn't a [development session](#development-sessions). In it the agent is a
guide: it runs fortkeep's own scripts and reads fortkeep's own files, and needs almost nothing else. So what it may do is
a short allow-list (`.claude/hooks/allow-list`), not a list of bad commands.

**Shell.** A command must be exactly one of fortkeep's entry points, run from the repo folder, spelled as the skills
write them, with arguments fortkeep validates:

- the check runner and its helpers in `checks/`: `run.sh`, `diff.sh`, `configure.sh`, `detect.sh`, `overlays.sh`,
  and `show.sh`, which prints a file under the read rules below (Codex has no read tool);
- `checks/ask.sh`, which prints the one question the person answers to approve something;
- `checks/accept.sh` and `checks/private.sh add` and `count`, which act only on the person's recorded answer (for a
  private folder, its answer to the question naming that folder);
- `checks/scan.sh`, which scans one folder the person names for signs of a poisoned repo: read-only, it runs nothing
  from the folder, and refuses a private folder, `/`, the home folder and the folders above it;
- `summary/name.sh` and `summary/build.sh`;
- `fixes/macos/<ID>.sh apply` and `undo`, which the agent asks before running. A fix is refused while the agent is in
  bypass, auto or accept-edits mode, where it would run without the person's prompt.

Everything else is refused: any other program, pipes, redirections, variables, command substitutions, globs, several
commands on one line, and characters beyond ASCII (except letters inside quotes in a name or a reason).

**Read tools** work only inside the fortkeep folder and the agent's own folders for this project (its scratch folder
and Claude Code's project folder, with memory and saved tool output). They never read `private-paths`,
`reports/.approvals`, `.git`, a file named as a secret (`.env`, `.env.*`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `id_*`, but not `*.example`)
or a file's named fork (`FILE/..namedfork/...`), and a search may not start at a folder that holds any of them. A
search pattern with braces (`{a,b}`) is refused, since an alternative could name a folder outside the one checked.
Private folders are outside the fortkeep folder, so read tools can't reach them at all: there is no name comparison
left to fool. The Artifact tool only publishes the summary page, `reports/latest/posture-summary.html`, as a new page
that stays private until the person shares it; any other file, action or destination is refused.
A guard that stops with any status but 0 or 2 (a crash, or a library that stops it) blocks the call: the agents go
ahead on any other status.

**Write tools** work only in this project's scratch folder and the plan folder. The plan folder holds every
project's plans, so it can't be read. Memory is never written: what lands there becomes standing instructions for
every later session. Nothing in the fortkeep folder is written either: `checks/configure.sh` saves the person's
settings and `checks/run.sh` writes results.

**Any other tool** is refused, in all three agents, except the ones that touch no file and run no command: the
question tool, the todo tools, skills, plan mode and Claude Code's tool loader. Web fetch and search are refused, since
a URL or query could carry what the agent read off the Mac; Codex's hosted web search reaches no hook, so
`.codex/config.toml` turns it off. Subagents and MCP tools are refused: their calls are not known to pass through the
guards.

What this closes: rewriting the guards, checks or fixes; committing to hide a change; forging an approval by any
spelling of its path; running a file dropped in `reports/`; starting another agent non-interactively to record an
approval; writing results by hand; and planting instructions in the agent's memory.

## Development sessions

Development sessions are for people changing fortkeep. One needs both `FORTKEEP_DEV=1` in the agent's environment and
the file `~/.config/fortkeep/dev`, which the person creates once in the Terminal app. The variable alone isn't enough:
a planted agent config or launcher can set it for commands no guard sees. The marker is read from the account's own
home folder, not `$HOME`, and no tool or script in a person's session writes there.

A development session keeps the older deny-list guards, which refuse known-bad commands and allow the rest and have
the [known limits](#known-limits) below, and the release checks let an untagged copy through.

## The approval

A fix runs only after the person answers `Apply <ID>` or `Undo <ID>`. Accepting an unmet control takes
`Accept <ID>`, and adding a private folder, which hides it from every check, takes `Add private folder`.

- **What it is.** A hook records the person's own answer: an option they picked in the agent's question tool, in
  exactly the question `checks/ask.sh` prints for that action, or, in Codex, a message that is exactly that answer.
  It writes a one-use token under `reports/.approvals`, which the script that acts on it consumes. A token expires
  after five minutes. The model can't write the person's messages, `guard.sh` refuses a question that arrives with
  its answers already filled in (only the model could have written them), a subagent's prompt records nothing, and in a
  person's session the model can't reach `reports/.approvals` by any tool. The hook records nothing when another agent
  started this one (`codex exec`, `claude -p` or `opencode run` inside a session). `checks/accept.sh` and
  `checks/private.sh add` need no token when the person types them in a terminal app.
- **What it isn't.** It is not a cryptographic proof. The token is a file the person's own account can write, so
  anything running as that user can make one. It shows that the person answered in a session where the guards ran;
  it does not show that the agent described the change honestly. The fix script and its lesson say what it changes.
- **An accepted control.** The question names the reason, and the token holds it: `checks/accept.sh` records only
  that reason, so the agent can't put its own words in the person's mouth. In Codex the typed answer carries it
  (`Accept <ID> <reason>`).
- **A private folder.** The question names the folder, in the one spelling `checks/private.sh` stores (absolute, no
  `.` or `..`), and the token holds that folder: `checks/private.sh add` takes only it. In Codex the typed answer
  names it (`Add private folder <path>`). `/`, the home folder (from `HOME` and from the account), a folder above
  it, and the fortkeep folder or a folder above it are never asked about or added from an agent's session, as spelled,
  with symlinks resolved or by physical path (`/System/Volumes/Data/Users/…` included), in any letter case. Hiding one would blind every check; the person can still add it in
  a terminal app.

## Checks

- Results come only from `checks/run.sh`. The agent never decides PASS or FAIL.
- A check never prints a secret's value: counts, lengths or fingerprints at most.
- A check never uses the network, with one exception: when this Mac's DNS servers aren't on BL-BR-06's known list, it
  looks up one published malware test name (and `example.com` only if that gets no answer) to see whether DNS
  filtering blocks it.
- Checks don't trust the environment they are started from. System folders come first on `PATH`, so a fake
  `fdesetup` earlier on it can't turn the FileVault check to PASS; checks that look at the person's tools read the
  person's own `PATH` for that. Checks run under `bash -p` with `BASH_ENV` and `ENV` unset, with no exported shell
  function, and `checks/run.sh` drops the test-only overrides outside the tests.
- Private folders are skipped by every check.

## Integrity

People's Macs run signed releases: version tags signed by a maintainer whose SSH key is in
`.github/allowed_signers`. [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md#verifying-a-release) shows how to verify one by hand.

- **What is checked.** Session start, the fix library, the weekly job and the scripts the person runs verify that the
  copy is a signed release with no local changes (`checks/update.sh`, which moves the copy onto one, checks only the
  changes). That covers every tracked file (content, type and executable bit),
  the untracked and ignored files where agents load configuration (`.claude/`, `.codex/`, `.agents/`, `.opencode/`,
  `opencode.json`, `.mcp.json` and local instruction files), git hooks, `info/attributes`, and local git settings
  that run a command or change what git reads. A failed check warns at session start and refuses everywhere else.
- **Who may sign.** A release counts only when a key this Mac trusts signed it: the signers of the first release it
  ran, then those each newer release names (`~/.config/fortkeep/release-signers`). A commit can't add its own signer.
- **Downgrades.** The highest release this Mac ran is recorded in `~/.config/fortkeep/highest-release`, so moving to an
  older one warns.
- **Updates.** `checks/update.sh` fetches only over https or ssh, and only from the place recorded at the first
  verified install (`~/.config/fortkeep/origin`); it refuses a copy that names another place, or several, and a
  `url.<base>.insteadOf` or `pushInsteadOf` setting, in the copy's git config or the person's own, that rewrites
  that place. Its messages never print an address, which can carry a token. It moves only to a release a trusted key
  signed, and once on a release only forward.
- **Where the record lives.** The origin, the trusted signers and the highest release are kept in the account's own
  home folder, read from the directory service, so a changed `HOME` can't point fortkeep at another record.
- **First install.** `install.sh` and the Homebrew formula pin one release by tag and commit. They refuse a clone whose
  tag isn't exactly that commit, check that before running anything from it, and refuse a tag that release's own
  signers didn't sign. That signature check adds little on its own: the pins are the trust root. They live on `main`
  (in `install.sh`, with its SHA-256 in the README) and in the tap repo (the formula), so whoever can change those
  decides what a fresh install gets. Branch protection on both, and the pins printed in each GitHub release's notes,
  are what guard them; [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md#verifying-a-release) shows how to check a release's signature by
  hand before installing. A plain `git clone` trusts `main` as it is that day until its first `checks/update.sh`.
- **Releases.** `make release` refuses a copy with local changes or with the extra files and git settings above. Git
  hooks are allowed to be there, since `make install` puts lefthook's in place, but the tag is made and removed with
  no hook folder (`core.hooksPath=/dev/null`), so none runs, `reference-transaction` included. It keeps the tag only if copies on the last release and fresh clones
  would both accept it. It checks this directly, because a maintainer runs it in development mode.
- **Not covered.** Files fortkeep installs outside its folder, such as the git scan hook and the weekly job's
  launcher, are not part of the signature check.

## Admin steps

- fortkeep never runs `sudo`. It gives the person the exact command to type in the Terminal app.
- Scripts the person runs around admin steps (`checks/baseline.sh accept`, `checks/managed-settings.sh`) verify the
  copy's integrity before they load anything else.
- `checks/managed-settings.sh` prints the files BL-AI-04 installs as root from the verified release, not from the
  working folder.

## Stated limits

- The guards are hooks, not a sandbox. They hold only while the agent program runs them.
- Codex runs them only after the person trusts the folder's hooks; OpenCode skips its plugin when started with
  `--pure`; other agents have none. Without them nothing is guarded, and no fix should run.
- Anything running as the person's user can change fortkeep's files, approvals and results.
- A first install trusts the pins on `main` or in the tap repo; a plain clone trusts `main` as it is that day, until
  its first `checks/update.sh`.
- A check reports only what it can read. A folder hidden by macOS privacy settings gives ERROR, not PASS.
- The repo sweep and the git scan hook find known campaigns by their indicators; a new campaign passes until its
  indicators are added.

## Known limits

- **Development-session guards** are pattern matching: they miss commands built from globs, names assembled from
  pieces, and shadowed shell functions.
- **The ready-made agent guard** (`templates/agent-guard.sh`) is pattern matching too, with the same gaps. It also
  refuses some harmless commands: a quoted separator next to a protected path, `sed` with a backslash, and Bash
  commands over 64 KB.
- **The terminal check** that keeps `checks/baseline.sh accept` for the person, and lets them run `checks/accept.sh`
  and `checks/private.sh add` without a token, is a tripwire: a renamed terminal binary, or a process that leaves the
  terminal's process tree, gets past it.
- **The process-tree check** counts an agent started by another of the same kind, with no shell between, as one
  agent, so the approval hook can't tell `codex exec` started directly by Codex from Codex itself. An npm launcher
  and the agent it starts must count as one, and agents start copies of themselves for their own work (Codex's
  app-server daemon runs `codex app-server` as its child, with the same executable); telling these apart would rest on
  each agent's undocumented process layout. It matters only when the first agent isn't guarded, since a person's
  session refuses starting another agent.
- **The test-suite switch** needs the environment the test helpers set, their marker file in the test's folder, and
  bats's test runner as an ancestor process. An agent config can set the variables and the agent's write tools can
  make the marker, but neither can make a process tree: a person's agent runs only fortkeep's scripts, which descend
  from the agent. It is also refused in the folders that agent may write (`/private/tmp/claude-*`, any `plans`
  folder). The runner is recognised by its script's path, so a launcher that starts the agent under a program at
  that path gets past it; such a launcher is a local change that session start reports.
- **Linked git hooks.** A file in a scanned repo's `.git/hooks` that links outside the repo is still read, to see
  whether it fetches or runs code. Only the rule it matched is printed, never its content.
- **Private folders by spelling.** Some older callers of `fortkeep_is_private`, `fortkeep_walk` among them, compare
  paths by spelling only, so a private folder reached through another spelling of its path may be read.
- **The weekly run** happens while the Mac is busy: OV-TP-02 can time out there, and BL-RC-03 can't read zsh aliases
  there.
- **Signed releases.** No test yet covers refusing a release tag signed with a PGP key instead of an SSH key.

# What fortkeep touches

Everything fortkeep reads, writes and sends over the network, and what a run may ask of macOS. It is for anyone
deciding whether to run it, and for anyone removing it.

## What it reads

The checks only read. Each lesson's "What the agent is doing" line (`teach/<ID>.md`) says exactly what its check
looks at. In short:

- **macOS settings:** FileVault, firewall, Gatekeeper, System Integrity Protection, software update preferences,
  sharing services, screen lock, `/etc/pam.d/sudo_local`, launchd's user PATH, and the DNS servers in use.
- **Installed apps and running programs:** names and versions of security tools (`/Applications`,
  `~/Applications`), the system extensions list, and the running processes' names, terminals, ages and working
  folders. GD-RT-03 also lists your own network connections, and reads the process list's command lines only to
  recognise a hidden node or python loader, never reporting them. Of the open apps' environment, only `PATH` is read.
- **Your start-up and tool configuration:** shell start-up files (`~/.zshrc`, `~/.zprofile`, `~/.zshenv`,
  `~/.zlogin`, `~/.bashrc`, `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.profile`), `~/.gitconfig` and its hooks, the npm, Yarn, pnpm,
  Bun, pip and uv config files, Safe Chain's files in `~/.safe-chain`, `~/.ssh/config`, and the key files in `~/.ssh`, which
  `ssh-keygen` tries to open with an empty passphrase to see whether each has one; no key is printed or kept.
- **Coding agents' settings:** Claude Code (`~/.claude`, `~/.claude.json`'s MCP servers, the managed settings in
  `/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode`), Codex (`~/.codex`, `/etc/codex/requirements.toml`), OpenCode, Zed,
  Cursor and the VS Code family's settings. The guards are sent test commands; nothing they would run is run.
- **Browsers:** each Chrome-family and Firefox profile's settings file, its extension list, and the number of
  passwords saved in it (a count; no password is opened).
- **Folders that may hold leaked keys or cloned repos:** the top of your home folder, and `~/Desktop`,
  `~/Documents` and `~/Downloads` (BL-SE-03, GD-RC-01), plus your code folders (GD-RC-01 lists them).
- **A folder you ask about:** `/scan` and `fortkeep scan` read the git repos in the one folder you name: their
  files (tracked or not, except node_modules), git hooks and commit history. Nothing from them runs.
- **fortkeep's own state:** everything listed under "What it writes" below.

Folders in `private-paths` are never read, listed or searched, by the checks or by the agent. When one is skipped,
the result says only "a private folder was excluded".

## What it writes

The installer (`install.sh`, or Homebrew's `fortkeep` on first run) puts the fortkeep folder at
`~/.local/share/fortkeep`, links `~/.local/bin/fortkeep` to its command when `~/.local/bin` exists, and records the
release it installed under `~/.config/fortkeep/`. A review (`checks/run.sh`) writes only inside fortkeep's own folders:

| Where | What |
|---|---|
| `reports/` in the fortkeep folder | settings (`config.json`), each run's `results.json`, the `latest` link, the posture summary, the KnockKnock scan, `weekly-last`, and `change-log.md` with every change a fix made |
| `reports/.approvals/` | the agent hooks' record of each `Apply`, `Undo` or `Accept` answer; never touched by hand |
| `accepted.json` and `private-paths` in the fortkeep folder | your accepted decisions and your private folders |
| `~/.config/fortkeep/` | accepted baselines (`baseline/`), the repo sweep's last result, and which signed release this Mac last ran and trusts |
| `~/.local/state/fortkeep/backups/` | a copy of each file a fix changed, so it can be undone |

A fix writes only after you answer `Apply <ID>`, and logs what it did in `reports/change-log.md` with its undo:

| Fix | What it writes |
|---|---|
| BL-SC-02 | `~/.config/fortkeep/path-front.sh`, and one marked line in `~/.zshenv`, `~/.zshrc`, `~/.zlogin` and your bash start-up files |
| BL-RC-01 | `"task.allowAutomaticTasks": "off"` in each VS Code-family editor's `settings.json` |
| BL-RC-02 | the scan hook at `~/.local/bin/git-scan-new-files`, hook entries in `~/.gitconfig`; the hook logs to `~/.local/var/log/git-scan.log` |
| BL-SE-06 | a gitleaks pre-commit hook entry in `~/.gitconfig` |
| BL-AU-02 | the weekly LaunchAgent `~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.github.b0dea.fortkeep.weekly.plist`, logging to `~/Library/Logs/fortkeep-weekly.log` |

Admin changes are typed by you in the Terminal app, never by the agent. The lessons give them: for example the
root-owned agent guard in `/usr/local/lib/safe-chain-agent/`, Claude Code's managed settings, Codex's
`/etc/codex/requirements.toml`, `/etc/pam.d/sudo_local`, launchd's user PATH, the firewall and Gatekeeper.

## Removing fortkeep

`fortkeep uninstall` does it in order, and never runs `sudo` or deletes the fortkeep folder itself:

1. It refuses while a fix that installed something is still applied: the scan hook, the gitleaks hook, the Safe
   Chain start-up lines or the weekly job. Undo each in your agent first (`fortkeep agent`, then ask it to undo the
   fix and answer `Undo <ID>`), so the backup puts your files back. The editor setting from BL-RC-01 may stay: it
   works without fortkeep.
2. It prints the admin changes below. They don't need fortkeep and keep protecting the Mac without it. To remove
   them anyway, type them yourself in the Terminal app, and only those you made from a fortkeep lesson, not ones your
   organisation installed:

   <!-- fortkeep-uninstall-admin:start -->
   ```sh
   sudo rm -f /usr/local/lib/safe-chain-agent/agent-guard.sh "/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json"
   sudo rm -f /etc/codex/requirements.toml
   sudo launchctl config user path "/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin"   # then restart the Mac
   sudo -k
   ```
   <!-- fortkeep-uninstall-admin:end -->

3. After you answer `yes`, it removes `~/.local/state/fortkeep` (fix backups), `~/.config/fortkeep` (baselines and
   release records) and the `~/.local/bin/fortkeep` link the installer made.
4. You delete the fortkeep folder yourself (by default `~/.local/share/fortkeep`), and run `brew uninstall fortkeep` if
   you installed it with Homebrew. The logs `~/.local/var/log/git-scan.log` and `~/Library/Logs/fortkeep-weekly.log`
   are yours to keep or delete.

## What it sends over the network

Checks are meant not to use the network, so a run says nothing about you to anyone. These are the exceptions:

- **BL-BR-06 (DNS filtering):** when the DNS servers aren't on its list of known filtering services, one DNS
  lookup of `malware.testcategory.com`, Cloudflare's published malware test name; only if that gets no answer at
  all, one lookup of `example.com` to tell a block from no network.
- **BL-SC-01 (Safe Chain installed):** runs Safe Chain's own `safe-chain-verify`, then asks npm, through Safe
  Chain, for Safe Chain's harmless test package in an empty temporary folder. That reaches the npm registry and
  Safe Chain's malware feed, as any install through Safe Chain does.
- **OV-TP-02 (only with the TLS-proxy set-up):** runs `safe-chain-verify` from a non-interactive shell, to see
  that it finishes behind your employer's proxy.
- **The installer:** clones fortkeep from GitHub (Homebrew also downloads the release's source archive).
- **`checks/update.sh` (`fortkeep update`):** fetches the release tags from fortkeep's git remote, only when you run
  it.
- **The weekly check (`checks/weekly.sh`):** `brew update`, then `brew vulns`, which use Homebrew's own servers.
  When KnockKnock is installed, its scan runs with VirusTotal turned off (`-skipVT`).

Nothing else is sent: no telemetry, no results, no file contents.

## macOS privacy prompts

The first run may make macOS ask whether your terminal or agent app may open the **Desktop**, **Documents** and
**Downloads** folders. BL-SE-03 looks there for leaked key files, and GD-RC-01 for cloned repos. Allowing it lets
those checks finish. If you decline, they report ERROR for that folder, and nothing else changes. You can change
your answer later in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Files and Folders.

## How long a run takes

Not measured on a reference Mac yet. The checks run one after another, each stopped at its own time limit (the
`timeout` of each control in `controls/controls.json`, or the default in `checks/run.sh`), and the run prints one
progress line per check. Expect minutes rather than seconds. The slowest check, the repo sweep (GD-RC-01), runs in
the weekly check; other reviews show its stored result.

## "Stopped from outside"

A result that says "Something outside fortkeep stopped this check" means another program ended the check before it
could answer. It is usually a security tool (antivirus or endpoint protection) mistaking a read-only check for
malware. It is not a sign that the Mac is unsafe, and that check simply has no answer this time.

What to do, and what not to ask for, is in [When a security tool stops a check](security-tools.md): an exclusion for
that one check, never for the fortkeep folder, and never turning the security tool off.

# BL-AI-01 · The agent's own shell finds npm at the Safe Chain shim

**Why:** Agents are suggestible and run with your credentials. A line of text in a README is enough to make one run an install. Safe Chain only stops that if the agent's own shell reaches the shims first.

**Real attack:** In May 2026 researchers showed that a booby-trapped README in a public repo, written as an error-fixing guide, made the Cursor coding agent print the developer's secret keys and send them to the attacker; the victim only had to point the agent at the repo. ([source](https://www.0din.ai/blog/stealing-environment-keys-from-cursor-ide-with-a-malicious-readme))

**Check it yourself:** ask the agent to run `/usr/bin/which npm` and `npm install --no-save safe-chain-test`. The first must print the shim; the second must be refused.

**How to fix:** fix BL-SC-02 and BL-SC-03, then quit the agent and start it again: it keeps the PATH it started with. Start it from the fortkeep folder as before and type `/fix` (in Codex, `$fix`); it checks the Mac again first.

**What the agent is doing:** asking where npm is in the shell this very review runs in, which is the agent's own.

# BL-AI-02 · A pre-command guard refuses package-manager bypasses

**Why:** The shims only work if the agent goes through them. A guard that runs before every agent command refuses the known ways around them: a package manager by full path, `PATH=` or `env -i` rewrites, `SAFE_CHAIN_*=0`, registry overrides, `curl … | sh`, running a "font" file with node, and edits to the files that enforce all this. It also refuses commands whose purpose is to print a secret into the agent's context (`varlock printenv`, `security find-generic-password -w`).

**Real attack:** A researcher found eight ways to make Claude Code run commands without asking the user, by slipping past its built-in check of "safe" commands; Anthropic fixed them in version 1.0.93 (CVE-2025-66032). The built-in check was not enough on its own, which is why a separate guard matters. ([source](https://flatt.tech/research/posts/pwning-claude-code-in-8-different-ways))

**Check it yourself:** in Claude Code or Codex, ask it to run `/opt/homebrew/bin/npm install left-pad`. It must be refused by a hook, not just declined politely.

**How to fix:** this repo ships a ready-made guard, `templates/agent-guard.sh`. Ask the agent to walk you through installing it. For Claude Code, you copy it to `~/.claude/hooks/` in Terminal and add it to your settings under `hooks.PreToolUse` for `Bash` and `Write|Edit|MultiEdit`. For Codex, you register the same guard in `~/.codex/hooks.json` as a `PreToolUse` hook for its shell commands and its file edits (`apply_patch`); the check tests both, and fails while Codex is installed without one. OpenCode: a plugin on `tool.execute.before`; Zed: `agent.tool_permissions.tools.terminal.always_deny`. The guard is pattern matching, not a sandbox: it stops an agent that slips or is talked into it. A repo's own `.claude/settings.json` can switch off your user-level hooks with `disableAllHooks`; only the managed copy (BL-AI-04) survives that.

**What the agent is doing:** sending each registered hook (Claude Code's settings, the managed copy, enabled plugins and Codex's `hooks.json`) a few test commands and one test file edit, never running or writing them, and checking which ones the hook refuses.

# BL-AI-03 · The agent can't edit its own controls

**Why:** Every control above lives in files your own user can write. An agent that can edit `~/.zshrc`, its own `settings.json` or the guard script can switch them off, and a convincing README can ask it to.

**Real attack:** In August 2026 the ChainDrop worm spread through npm packages and wrote a hook into repositories' `.claude/settings.json` (and a VS Code task), so its code runs again each time someone starts Claude Code or opens the project. ([source](https://www.pillar.security/blog/chaindrop-when-opening-a-repository-becomes-execution), [source](https://zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/tracking-shai-hulud-inside-chaindrop-npm-worm))

**Check it yourself:** open your Claude Code `settings.json` and look under `permissions.deny` for `Edit(…)` entries covering that file, your shell start-up files and the guard script. For Codex, ask it to edit `~/.codex/config.toml`: a hook must refuse.

**How to fix:** add to `permissions.deny` in your Claude Code `settings.json`: `"Edit(~/.zshrc)"`, `"Edit(~/.zprofile)"`, `"Edit(~/.zshenv)"`, `"Edit(~/.zlogin)"`, `"Edit(~/.bashrc)"`, `"Edit(~/.bash_profile)"` (each one only if that file exists), `"Edit(/settings.json)"` (the file itself), one for the guard script, and `"Edit(~/.config/fortkeep/**)"` if you have `~/.config/fortkeep/path-front.sh` (the file that puts the Safe Chain shims first, from BL-SC-02). Use only `Edit(…)` rules: they cover every file-editing tool. Codex has no deny rules: there, the guard registered in `~/.codex/hooks.json` for its file edits (`apply_patch`, see BL-AI-02) must refuse an edit to `hooks.json` itself, `config.toml`, its rules files, the guard script and your shell start-up files. Never accept a security baseline from an agent.

**What the agent is doing:** reading your Claude Code deny rules and matching them against the files that need protecting, and, for Codex, sending its file-edit hook a test edit of each of those files (never writing it) to see that the hook refuses.

# BL-AI-04 · A root-owned copy of the agent controls the agent can't reach

**Why:** Every control in BL-AI-02 and BL-AI-03 lives in files your own user can write, so an agent running as you can, in principle, undo them. A copy owned by root, which managed settings make win over user and project settings, can't be changed without your admin password. Deny rules there apply even with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`.

**Real attack:** Check Point showed that a hook in a cloned repo's own `.claude/settings.json` ran a command as soon as the user accepted the trust prompt (fixed in 2025). Settings the repo or your user can write can be changed by whatever you open; Claude Code's admin-managed settings can block user, project and plugin hooks, and a repo can't switch those off. ([source](https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/rce-and-api-token-exfiltration-through-claude-code-project-files-cve-2025-59536/), [source](https://workos.com/blog/npm-worm-coding-agent-config-credentials))

**Check it yourself:** `ls -l "/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json"` shows `root wheel`, and the file contains `"disableBypassPermissionsMode": "disable"` and a hook pointing at a script under `/usr/local/lib`. For Codex, `ls -l /etc/codex/requirements.toml` shows `root wheel`, and the file allows only `read-only` and `workspace-write`.

**How to fix:** this needs your admin password. Open the Terminal app (Applications → Utilities), go to the fortkeep folder (`cd` and a space, then the folder), and type each step on its own, pressing Return after each.

For Claude Code:
1. `t="$(mktemp -d)"` makes a temporary folder for two files.
2. `checks/managed-settings.sh guard > "$t/agent-guard.sh"` saves the guard script, taken from the signed release.
3. `checks/managed-settings.sh > "$t/managed-settings.json"` saves the settings, with a rule for every other Claude Code folder it finds (such as your `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, if you use one: type this where that is set).
4. `jq -e '.permissions.deny | length > 0' "$t/managed-settings.json"` must print `true`. If it prints anything else, or step 2 or 3 said REFUSED, stop and tell the agent what you saw.
5. `sudo mkdir -p /usr/local/lib/safe-chain-agent "/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode"`. macOS asks for your password; nothing appears on screen while you type it, which is normal.
6. `sudo install -o root -g wheel -m 755 "$t/agent-guard.sh" /usr/local/lib/safe-chain-agent/agent-guard.sh`
7. `sudo install -o root -g wheel -m 644 "$t/managed-settings.json" "/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json"`
8. `sudo -k`, which ends the admin session.

For Codex, which reads its root-owned rules from `/etc/codex/requirements.toml`:
1. `sudo mkdir -p /etc/codex`
2. `echo 'allowed_sandbox_modes = ["read-only", "workspace-write"]' | sudo tee /etc/codex/requirements.toml`
3. `sudo -k`

After each fortkeep update, repeat the Claude Code steps: this check compares the root-owned guard with your own copy of the same name and fails while they differ. Keep the agent autonomous: the point is a filter on what it installs and which files it touches, not approving every command. Codex's `workspace-write` mode still works on its own inside your project; only switching its sandbox off entirely (`danger-full-access`) is ruled out. Don't set `allowManagedHooksOnly` unless every hook you rely on is in the managed file. This protects against the agent, not against someone with your admin password.

**What the agent is doing:** reading the managed settings file and Codex's requirements, checking who owns them and the hook script, and comparing that script with your own copy. The agent never runs sudo.

# BL-AI-05 · MCP servers pinned to a version

**Why:** An MCP server starts every time the agent starts. `npx -y some-server` fetches whatever version is newest at that moment, so a hijacked release runs on your next session, with the agent's access.

**Real attack:** In September 2025 a fake copy of Postmark's email MCP server on npm behaved normally for 15 versions, then version 1.0.16 quietly copied every email it sent to an outside address. Anyone pinned to an earlier version never received that change. ([source](https://www.theregister.com/2025/09/29/postmark_mcp_server_code_hijacked/))

**Check it yourself:** in your Claude Code MCP config (`claude mcp list`, or `~/.claude.json`), every `npx`, `uvx`, `bunx` or `pnpm dlx` server names an exact version: `pkg@1.2.3` or `pkg==1.2.3`.

**How to fix:** for each server the agent names, look up the version you're using and pin it: remove and re-add it with `claude mcp add … -- npx -y pkg@1.2.3`. Update deliberately, not automatically.

**What the agent is doing:** reading your MCP server list and reporting only the names of unpinned servers. Their arguments and settings, which can hold tokens, are never shown.

# BL-AI-06 · The agent's sandbox on (Claude Code, Codex)

**Why:** The sandbox (macOS Seatbelt) limits, at kernel level, where the agent's commands can write and which network destinations they can reach. It's a stronger fence than pattern-matching hooks. By default it doesn't stop them reading your files: to keep `~/.ssh` or `~/.aws/credentials` out of reach, add a deny rule for reading them.

**Real attack:** The ChainDrop worm of August 2026 collected SSH keys from `~/.ssh` and other credentials and sent them out. Claude Code's sandbox only lets commands reach websites you have allowed, so the sending step is blocked; reading `~/.ssh` is allowed unless you add a deny rule for it. ([source](https://zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/tracking-shai-hulud-inside-chaindrop-npm-worm), [source](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing))

**Check it yourself:** your Claude Code `settings.json` (or the managed one) has `"sandbox": {"enabled": true}`. Codex sandboxes its commands unless `~/.codex/config.toml` sets `sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"`.

**How to fix:** in Claude Code, add that setting, then expect breakage: `docker`, `gh`, `terraform` and `osascript` usually need exclusions, and the loop is slower. That trade-off is why this is NICE, not MUST. In Codex, remove the `danger-full-access` line (or choose `workspace-write`).

**What the agent is doing:** reading the sandbox setting in Claude Code's settings and Codex's `config.toml`.

# BL-AU-01 · A weekly update job runs

**Why:** Security tools and packages only help while they're current. A weekly job that upgrades your Homebrew packages keeps that from depending on memory.

**Real attack:** US government agencies reported that in 2022 attackers exploited older, already-fixed software flaws more often than new ones, because many organisations hadn't installed the fixes. ([source](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-215a))

**Check it yourself:** `launchctl list | grep -i weekly` shows your job, and its log shows a recent run.

**How to fix:** fortkeep's own weekly security check (BL-AU-02) doesn't count here: it runs `brew update` and tells you when a formula has a vulnerability with a released fix, but it never upgrades anything. This control needs a job that runs `brew upgrade` itself.

Save this as `~/.local/bin/weekly-update.sh` and make it executable (`chmod +x`):

    #!/bin/zsh
    export PATH=/opt/homebrew/bin:/usr/local/bin:$PATH
    { date; brew update && brew upgrade && brew vulns --fix-available; } 2>&1

Then create a LaunchAgent in `~/Library/LaunchAgents` that runs it every Monday (the agent can write the plist with you), and load it with `launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) <plist>`.

**What the agent is doing:** looking through your own LaunchAgents for a weekly job whose command or script runs `brew upgrade`, leaving out fortkeep's own weekly check, and checking that it's loaded.

# BL-AU-02 · A weekly security check runs and is up to date

**Why:** Settings drift: an update resets something, a new tool adds a login item, a hook gets removed. A weekly review that notifies you when something newly fails catches it within days.

**Real attack:** In a 2022 refund scam against US federal staff, attackers used the remote-support tools AnyDesk and ScreenConnect; US agencies note that this kind of software generally doesn't trigger antivirus alerts, so only a regular look at what is installed and running will catch it. ([source](https://www.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa23-025a))

**Check it yourself:** `launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/io.github.b0dea.fortkeep.weekly` shows the job, and `/posture` says your last review was within the week.

**How to fix:** The agent can install it (`fixes/macos/BL-AU-02.sh apply`). Every Wednesday at 10:00 it runs a KnockKnock scan (if installed) and a full review from this repo, then `brew update` and a report of formulae with a vulnerability that has a released fix (it never upgrades). It logs to `~/Library/Logs/fortkeep-weekly.log`, and shows a notification if something newly fails. It runs this repo's own scripts, so update it only with `checks/update.sh`: it refuses to run, notifies you and logs why when tracked files have local changes.

**What the agent is doing:** checking that the job exists and is loaded, and how long ago the weekly job last ran its review.

# BL-BR-01 · Browsers' built-in password manager off

**Why:** Chrome-family browsers and Firefox keep saved passwords in files on disk. Stealers know exactly where, and decrypt them after one Keychain prompt or a fake password dialog. A locked password manager vault (1Password, Bitwarden, or Apple's Passwords app, which keeps them in the Keychain) gives them far less.

**Real attack:** Trend Micro analysed an AMOS stealer infection that showed a fake "System Preferences" password box, kept asking until the real Mac password was typed, and copied saved logins from browsers including Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Brave, Opera and Vivaldi. ([source](https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/an-mdr-analysis-of-the-amos-stealer-campaign.html))

**Check it yourself:** Chrome → Settings → Autofill and passwords → Google Password Manager → Settings → "Offer to save passwords" off. Firefox → Settings → Privacy & Security → "Ask to save passwords" off. Then delete the saved passwords after moving them to your password manager.

**How to fix:** move your saved passwords into your password manager (1Password, Bitwarden and Apple's Passwords app can import them), switch off saving in each browser and profile the agent names, then delete what's still saved there. Turning saving off doesn't delete what's saved: the check fails while any saved password is left in a browser profile, and names how many. Safari isn't checked, and Apple Passwords users pass: those passwords are in the Keychain, not a browser file.

**What the agent is doing:** reading one setting in each browser profile's settings file, and counting the saved passwords in each profile's password file. It counts rows only; it never opens or reads a password.

# BL-BR-02 · A password manager extension in every browser profile (1Password, Bitwarden or iCloud Passwords)

**Why:** A password manager's extension fills a password only on the site it belongs to, so a look-alike phishing site gets nothing, and you never need the browser's own password store.

**Real attack:** Phishing pages copy real login pages exactly. 1Password says its autofill only works on the exact domains your logins are saved for, so on a look-alike site it offers nothing, which is your warning. ([source](https://support.1password.com/kb/202508))

**Check it yourself:** your password manager's icon is in each browser's toolbar, in every profile.

**How to fix:** install your password manager's extension from your browser's extension store in each profile the agent names, and sign in: 1Password (paid), Bitwarden (free), or iCloud Passwords if you use Apple's Passwords app (Chrome, Edge and Firefox). Safari needs no extension. If you use another password manager, tell the agent to record it as your decision (ACCEPTED) with its name as the reason.

**What the agent is doing:** listing each profile's turned-on extensions by id and name.

# BL-BR-03 · uBlock Origin or Brave shields in every browser profile

**Why:** Malicious ads ("malvertising") push fake download pages for popular tools to the top of search results. A content blocker removes them, and with them a common way stealers get installed.

**Real attack:** In September 2023 Malwarebytes found Google search ads for the TradingView charting app that led to a look-alike download site; its Mac button delivered the AMOS stealer. ([source](https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/threat-intel/2023/09/atomic-macos-stealer-delivered-via-malvertising))

**Check it yourself:** the uBlock Origin icon is in each browser's toolbar (in Brave, the shields are built in).

**How to fix:** install uBlock Origin (Firefox) or uBlock Origin Lite (Chrome and Edge) in each profile the agent names, or use Brave with shields on.

**What the agent is doing:** listing each profile's installed extensions by id and name.

# BL-BR-04 · No crypto wallet extensions on this Mac

**Why:** Wallet extensions are the first thing a stealer goes for. Their vaults sit in the browser profile folder, and one stolen seed phrase empties the wallet for good.

**Real attack:** BeaverTail, malware North Korean attackers hide in fake job-interview coding tests, searches browser profiles for crypto wallet extension folders (MetaMask, Phantom, Binance Wallet, Coinbase Wallet) and sends what it finds back to the attacker. ([source](https://socket.dev/blog/2025-blockchain-and-cryptocurrency-threat-report), [source](https://www.atlassian.com/blog/how-we-build/disrupting-contagious-interview))

**Check it yourself:** look through each browser's extensions page for wallets, and remove any extension you don't use.

**How to fix:** move crypto to a hardware wallet (Ledger, Trezor) or a separate device, then remove the extension. If you hold crypto, keep it off the machine where you run other people's code.

**What the agent is doing:** listing installed extensions by id and name and matching them against known wallets.

# BL-BR-05 · A separate browser profile for development

**Why:** Development means visiting unknown repos, docs and demo sites and installing developer extensions. A separate profile with no personal logins keeps that away from your email, bank and social accounts.

**Real attack:** In December 2024 attackers phished a Chrome extension maker and pushed a poisoned update of the Cyberhaven extension that was built to steal cookies and access tokens from the sites you visit; the same attack hit other extensions. An extension only sees the profile it is installed in. ([source](https://securityaffairs.com/172491/hacking/chrome-browser-extensions-compromise.html))

**Check it yourself:** your browser's profile menu shows at least two profiles, one used only for development.

**How to fix:** create a new profile (Chrome: profile icon → Add; Firefox: `about:profiles`) and use it only for development, without signing in to personal accounts.

**What the agent is doing:** counting browser profiles. It can't tell which one you use for what.

# BL-BR-06 · DNS filtering with malware blocklists

**Why:** Filtering DNS refuses to look up known malware, phishing and command-and-control domains, so many attacks fail at the first connection.

**Real attack:** The UK's National Cyber Security Centre runs a filtering DNS service that refuses to look up known-malicious domains, because malware on an infected machine normally finds its controller through a DNS lookup, and so does a clicked phishing link; when the lookup is refused, the connection never starts. ([source](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/pdfs/information/pdns.pdf))

**Check it yourself:** System Settings → Network → your connection → Details → DNS shows 1.1.1.2 and 1.0.0.2 (or Quad9's or NextDNS's servers). For any other set-up, `dscacheutil -q host -a name malware.testcategory.com` in the Terminal app should print no address: that name is Cloudflare's published malware test name.

**How to fix:** set your DNS servers to `1.1.1.2` and `1.0.0.2` (Cloudflare with malware blocking, free) or `9.9.9.9` (Quad9, free), or use NextDNS (paid, with a free tier) with its malware blocklists on.

**What the agent is doing:** reading which DNS servers macOS uses. If they aren't on its list of known filtering services, it makes one DNS lookup of `malware.testcategory.com` and passes if your DNS blocks it; only if that gets no answer at all, it looks up `example.com` to tell a block from no network. `docs/what-fortkeep-touches.md` lists every network use.

# BL-IS-01 · A VM or container tool for untrusted code

**Why:** Interview take-homes, "please review my code" zips and random GitHub projects are how developer Macs get owned. Run them in a throwaway VM or container with only that folder mounted: no home folder, no keys, no logins. The baseline makes never running them on your main account a MUST.

**Real attack:** North Korean attackers pose as recruiters and send developers a take-home coding test hidden with malware that can steal credentials, crypto wallets and API tokens; a November 2026 report on the PolinRider campaign describes the same lure, and Atlassian advises running such tests only in an isolated environment. ([source](https://www.atlassian.com/blog/how-we-build/disrupting-contagious-interview), [source](https://abnormal.ai/blog/polinrider-fake-coding-assignments))

**Check it yourself:** OrbStack, UTM, Docker Desktop, Colima or similar is installed, and you actually use it for code you didn't write.

**How to fix:** install OrbStack (free for personal use; paid for work) or UTM (free). Use dev containers for repos you work on often but didn't write, and a separate macOS user account for anything truly sketchy.

**What the agent is doing:** looking for known VM and container apps and commands.

# BL-OS-01 · FileVault on

**Why:** FileVault encrypts the whole disk. If the Mac is lost or stolen, nobody can read your files without your password.

**Real attack:** In 2011 the UK data regulator fined Ealing and Hounslow councils £80,000 and £70,000 after two laptops were stolen from an employee's home; they had passwords but weren't encrypted. The regulator said password protection "is simply not enough". ([source](https://www.itpro.com/630847/london-councils-fined-150000-for-unencrypted-laptop-thefts))

**Check it yourself:** run `fdesetup isactive` in Terminal. It prints `true` when FileVault is on.

**How to fix:** System Settings → Privacy & Security → FileVault → Turn On. Store the recovery key in your password manager, not in a file on this Mac. Encryption finishes in the background; keep working.

**What the agent is doing:** reading a single on/off status. It can't turn FileVault on for you: that click is yours, by design.

# BL-OS-02 · Firewall on with stealth mode

**Why:** The firewall stops other devices on the same network from connecting to services on your Mac. Stealth mode makes the Mac ignore probes, so it is harder to find at all.

**Real attack:** The DarkHotel campaign targeted business travellers on hotel Wi-Fi, prompting guests to install fake software updates after they logged in with their room number. Kaspersky concluded that public and semi-public hotel Wi-Fi is not safe, so don't let your Mac answer other devices there. ([source](https://www.kaspersky.com/blog/the-dark-story-of-darkhotel/15022/))

**Check it yourself:** `/usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --getglobalstate --getstealthmode`

**How to fix:** needs your admin password. Open the Terminal app (Applications → Utilities) and type these, one at a time, pressing Return after each:

1. `sudo /usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --setglobalstate on`. macOS asks for your password; nothing appears on screen while you type it, which is normal.
2. `sudo /usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --setstealthmode on`
3. `sudo -k`, which ends the admin session.

Or click: System Settings → Network → Firewall → on, then Options → Enable stealth mode.

**What the agent is doing:** The agent never runs `sudo` itself. You run admin commands, so you always see exactly what gets admin rights.

# BL-OS-03 · Gatekeeper on

**Why:** Gatekeeper refuses to open apps that aren't signed and checked by Apple, unless you explicitly allow them.

**Real attack:** In 2023 fake TradingView ads led to a Mac download whose instructions told people how to get past Gatekeeper; it installed the AMOS stealer, which kept asking for the Mac password until it was typed. ([source](https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/threat-intel/2023/09/atomic-macos-stealer-delivered-via-malvertising))

**Check it yourself:** `spctl --status` prints `assessments enabled`.

**How to fix:** needs your admin password. Open the Terminal app (Applications → Utilities) and type these, one at a time, pressing Return after each:

1. `sudo spctl --global-enable`. macOS asks for your password; nothing appears on screen while you type it, which is normal.
2. `sudo -k`, which ends the admin session.

Then never paste a command from a website that mentions `spctl`, `xattr` or "disable".

**What the agent is doing:** reading Gatekeeper's status. If you ever see instructions (from anyone, including an AI) to disable it, stop and ask.

# BL-OS-04 · System Integrity Protection on

**Why:** SIP stops anything, even with admin rights, from changing core macOS files. Malware that can't touch the system can't hide in it.

**Real attack:** In 2021 Microsoft found a macOS bug, "Shrootless", that let an attacker get around SIP and then install a rootkit (malware that hides deep in the system) or overwrite system files; Apple fixed it in October 2021. Microsoft calls SIP the Mac's "last line of defense" against malware. ([source](https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2021/10/28/microsoft-finds-new-macos-vulnerability-shrootless-that-could-bypass-system-integrity-protection/))

**Check it yourself:** `csrutil status` prints `System Integrity Protection status: enabled.`

**How to fix:** SIP can only be turned on from macOS Recovery:
1. Shut down. On Apple silicon, press and hold the power button until "Loading startup options" appears, then choose Options. On Intel, restart holding ⌘R.
2. Utilities → Terminal, type `csrutil enable`, press Return.
3. Restart.
4. To come back afterwards: open the Terminal app, type `cd` and a space followed by the fortkeep folder, press Return, start your coding agent as before and type `/fix` (in Codex, `$fix`). It checks the Mac again first.

**What the agent is doing:** reading SIP's status. The agent can't reach Recovery; you do these steps yourself and tell the agent when you're back.

# BL-OS-05 · Automatic updates on, including security responses

**Why:** Most attacks on Macs use bugs Apple has already fixed. Updates only protect you once they're installed.

**Real attack:** In December 2025 Apple fixed two bugs in WebKit, the engine behind Safari, which it said may have been used in an "extremely sophisticated attack" on specific people; the fixes shipped for Mac in macOS Tahoe 26.2 and Safari 26.2, and the US cyber agency listed both as exploited. ([source](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2025/12/15/ios-macos-cve-2025-14174-cve-2025-43529/))

**Check it yourself:** System Settings → General → Software Update → the (i) next to Automatic Updates.

**How to fix:** in that panel, turn on: Check for updates, Download new updates when available, Install Security Responses and system files. Installing macOS updates automatically is recommended too. On macOS 26 (Tahoe), Apple ships urgent fixes between updates as Background Security Improvements, which replaced Rapid Security Responses: in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Background Security Improvements, keep "Automatically Install" on. The check doesn't read that switch yet, so look at it yourself.

**What the agent is doing:** reading four update preferences. "default" in the evidence means you've never changed it, and macOS keeps it on. Settings your organisation manages through a device-management profile aren't read yet.

# BL-OS-06 · Sharing services off

**Why:** Each sharing service listens for connections from the network. Services you don't use are doors left unlocked.

**Real attack:** In August 2026 attackers broke into Macs whose Screen Sharing port was reachable from the internet, using a flaw (CVE-2026-65400) that let them in without a password, and planted a crypto miner; Apple's fix shipped on 6 August. ([source](https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/apple-macos-screen-sharing-flaw.html))

**Check it yourself:** System Settings → General → Sharing: everything off unless you use it this week. General → AirDrop & Handoff: AirPlay Receiver off.

**How to fix:** switch those off in the same panels. Nothing breaks: you can turn one back on the day you need it.

**What the agent is doing:** listing which network ports are open (not what's sent over them) and reading the AirPlay Receiver setting.

# BL-OS-07 · Screen locks immediately

**Why:** An unlocked, unattended laptop gives anyone your logged-in sessions: email, GitHub, cloud consoles, password manager.

**Real attack:** An IBM security tester who is paid to break into offices says that with an unattended company laptop he gets access to every document its owner can reach, can send phishing emails as them and can plant files in company folders. ([source](https://ibm.com/think/insights/physical-cybersecurity))

**Check it yourself:** System Settings → Lock Screen → "Require password after screen saver begins or display is turned off".

**How to fix:** set it to Immediately. Habit to go with it: ⌃⌘Q locks the screen whenever you stand up.

**What the agent is doing:** reading the lock delay with `sysadminctl`; it changes nothing.

# BL-OS-08 · Touch ID for sudo

**Why:** Typing your admin password into a terminal over and over invites shoulder-surfing and lets anything recording keystrokes capture it. Touch ID proves you're physically there.

**Real attack:** Trend Micro found the AMOS stealer showing a "System Preferences" box that asked for the Mac password and kept reappearing until it was entered, then saved the real password to a hidden file. With Touch ID for sudo you rarely type that password, so an unexpected prompt stands out. ([source](https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/an-mdr-analysis-of-the-amos-stealer-campaign.html))

**Check it yourself:** `cat /etc/pam.d/sudo_local` shows an uncommented `auth sufficient pam_tid.so` line.

**How to fix:** needs your admin password once. If `/etc/pam.d/sudo_local` doesn't exist yet, open the Terminal app (Applications → Utilities) and type these, one at a time, pressing Return after each:

1. `sudo sh -c 'sed "s/^#auth/auth/" /etc/pam.d/sudo_local.template > /etc/pam.d/sudo_local'`. macOS asks for your password; nothing appears on screen while you type it, which is normal.
2. `sudo -k`, which ends the admin session.
